Ayat 25–26 give the cosmic scene: the heavens torn open, angels descending, and every claim to sovereignty collapsing except one. Ayat 27–29 close in on one man inside that scene, biting his own hands with regret over two things — the path he refused, and the friend he chose. The rendering given in Ibn Kathir opens both scenes with the same words — **"And (remember) the Day…"** — so that the terror outside is set beside a discovery inside: that a friendship cost a man everything.

## Ayah 25 — the sky opened, the angels sent down

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us here of "the terror of the Day of Resurrection and the tremendous events that will happen," among them the splitting of the heavens when they are pierced by the clouds — and he identifies that cloud as the shadow of the magnificent light which dazzles all sight. The angels of heaven will then come down on that Day and surround all creatures at the place of gathering, and then, he says, "the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, will come to pass judgement." Mujahid connected this ayah to another: *"Do they then wait for anything other than that Allah should come to them in the shadows of the clouds and the angels"* (2:210).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Bayan ul-Qurʼan) fills in the picture. The sky will rip apart and a sort of cloud will descend from it carrying the angels with it — like a canopy coming down from the sky, bearing Allah's refulgence, surrounded by angels. Two points of sequencing follow. First, this will precede the beginning of the reckoning; it is the opening scene of judgement, not its verdict. Second, this ripping is not the same ripping as the one when the *ṣūr* (the Trumpet) is blown to finish off the earth and the sky. Here the sky rips open only to make an opening, and this descent of the cloud takes place *after* the second blowing of the Trumpet, once the earth and the sky have taken their new shape.

The rendering itself strains to hold the scale of it: the angels are not merely sent down, but "sent down, with a grand descending."

## Ayah 26 — "True authority that Day belongs to the Most Compassionate"

Every sovereignty that ever existed in this world was borrowed and provisional. On that Day the ownership is stated plainly and exclusively. Ibn Kathir pairs the ayah with *"Whose is the kingdom this Day? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible!"* (40:16), and then quotes a report he introduces simply as "In the Sahih": that Allah, may He be exalted, will fold up the heavens in His Right Hand and will take the earths in His other Hand, then He will say, *"I am the Sovereign, I am the Judge. Where are the kings of the earth? Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogants?"*

Notice, too, whose sovereignty the ayah names: **ar-Raḥmān**, the Most Compassionate. The commentators here simply let the Name stand; the pause is mine — that the Day of decisive judgement is announced under the Name of mercy.

**"And it will be a hard Day for the disbelievers."** Ibn Kathir explains this to mean "it will be very difficult," and gives the reason: because it will be the Day of justice and the decisive judgement — hard precisely because nothing on it will be crooked. He cites *"Truly, that Day will be a hard Day — far from easy for the disbelievers"* (74:9–10), and then draws the line the ayah itself draws by naming only the disbelievers: as for the believers, *"The greatest terror will not grieve them"* (21:103). The same Day, two utterly different experiences.

## Ayah 27 — the wrongdoer bites his hands

The scene narrows. Ibn Kathir describes the man as one "who rejected the path of the Messenger and what he brought from Allah of clear truth concerning which there is no doubt, and followed another path." When the Day of Resurrection comes the regret finally lands — but, in Ibn Kathir's words, "his regret will avail him nothing, and he will bite on his hands in sorrow and grief."

The ayah says he bites *his two hands*; the translation given renders it "bite his nails," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes him biting his fingers in distress and repentance. The picture is of a man turning his own violence inward because there is no longer anything outward left to do — no argument to make, no companion to appeal to, no time to spend. That last observation is my own reading of the image, not a claim from the commentaries.

Notice, too, what he wishes for. Not simply a path: **"a path with the Messenger."** What he mourns is a road he could have walked in someone's company, and did not.

Ibn Kathir is careful about the identity of this wrongdoer: "Whether this Ayah was revealed concerning ʿUqbah bin Abi Muʿīṭ or someone else among the doomed, **it applies to every wrongdoer**." He compares it to *"On the Day when their faces will be turned over in the Fire"* (33:66). Every wrongdoer, he says, will feel the ultimate regret on the Day of Resurrection, and will bite at his hands saying exactly these words.

## Ayah 28 — the story behind "so-and-so"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the occasion of revelation — noting that the verse was revealed on a particular occasion but that its implication is universal — and it is the key that unlocks the whole passage.

ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayṭ was one of the chieftains of the polytheists in Makkah. Whenever he returned from an expedition he would invite the nobility of the city to dinner, and he used to call on the Prophet ﷺ frequently. On one such occasion he presented food to the Prophet ﷺ, who said he could not eat it until ʿUqbah proclaimed that Allah is One with no one associated with Him in worship, and that he ﷺ is His Messenger. ʿUqbah recited the words, and the Prophet ﷺ ate the dinner according to his promise.

Then his close friend heard about it. ʿUbayy ibn Khalaf was very cross that ʿUqbah had accepted Islam and recited the Kalimah. ʿUqbah tried to defend himself: Muhammad ﷺ was an eminent person of Quraysh, and for him to leave the house without eating would have been degrading for the host — the words were said only to please him. ʿUbayy would not accept the explanation, and told ʿUqbah that if he was really ashamed he should go and spit on the Prophet's ﷺ face. The wretched man obliged his depraved friend and did as suggested.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, on the authority of Baghawi, that Allah disgraced them both in this world as well, both being killed at the battle of Badr — and that this ayah describes the torment awaiting such a man on the Day of Judgement: seeing the torment before him, he bites his fingers in distress and repentance and wishes he had never made ʿUbayy ibn Khalaf his friend in the world. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this account with the attribution "Mazhari, Qurtubi.")

Sit with the shape of it. ʿUqbah's tongue had already formed the truth. What undid him, on this account, was not an argument, not evidence, not doubt about the message — it was a friend's contempt.

## Why the Qur'an says "so-and-so" and not a name

The ayah does not name ʿUbayy. It says **fulān** — "so-and-so." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Tafsir Mazhari, points precisely at this: although these verses were revealed in respect of ʿUqbah, the moral of the verse is universal, and the use of the word *fulān* is what alludes to that universality.

The classical scholars did differ over the identity behind the blank. Ibn Kathir leaves it open — "whether this refers to Umayyah bin Khalaf or his brother Ubayy bin Khalaf, or to someone else" — and defines the man by his function rather than his name: "the one among the propagators of misguidance who diverted him from true guidance and led him to follow the path of misguidance." The sources Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows name ʿUbayy ibn Khalaf specifically. Either way, by the Qur'an's own choice of *fulān*, the lesson is not confined to one man's history.

## Ayah 29 — "He led me astray from the Reminder"

**"The Reminder"** — *adh-dhikr* — means the Qur'an, says Ibn Kathir; and "after it had come to me" means, in his words, "after it had reached me." This is the sharpest edge of the passage. The man's ruin was not that the truth never arrived. It arrived, and reached him.

Then the ayah closes with a line the wrongdoer does not say — Allah says it: **"And Shaytan is to man ever a deserter."** Ibn Kathir explains the work Shaytan does: "he leads him away from the truth and diverts him from it, and uses him for the purposes of falsehood and calls him to it." The classical rendering adds a clarifying phrase to the word: a deserter *"(in the hour of need)."*

There is something quietly striking in the placement — and here I am reflecting rather than reporting: the man spends ayah 28 blaming his friend, and Allah's own comment is not a denial but a widening, so that behind the human friend stands the one who deserts a person exactly when he is needed.

## From the Sunnah — on choosing company

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical lesson: when two friends get together in acts of immorality and sin and help each other in performing forbidden deeds, the same will apply to them, and they will be remorseful and feel sorry for their friendship in the Hereafter. It then cites three narrations:

- **Musnad Ahmed, Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud** and others, on the authority of Sayyidna Abu Saʿid al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ once said, in the rendering given: "Do not make a non-Muslim your friend and your possessions should be used only by the pious persons." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses the point as: do not have the non-pious as your friend.
- **Bukhari**, reported from Sayyidna Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), rendered: "Every person is influenced by the faith and way of life of his friends." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the consequence — "therefore, one must be very mindful when selecting his friends." The narration's word for the friend, *khalīl*, is the very word ayah 28 uses.
- **al-Bazzar**, reported from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and given with the attribution "Qurtubi": the Prophet ﷺ was asked what sort of friends we should keep in our company, and answered — "The one who reminds you of Allah when you see him, and adds to your knowledge when he speaks, and reminds you of the Hereafter when he acts."

Read that last narration beside ayah 28 and the contrast is hard to miss. On the account Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives, ʿUbayy was the exact inverse of that description at every point.

## Living it

What follows is application and personal reflection rather than commentary from the sources.

The passage puts one concrete question in front of a reader: **who is your fulān?** Not who is your enemy — the ayah is not about enemies. It is about a *khalīl*, an intimate friend: the person whose disapproval is hardest to bear.

Three things follow.

First, the regrets in ayat 27 and 28 look like one regret seen from two sides. "Would that I had taken a path with the Messenger" and "would that I had never taken so-and-so as an intimate friend" sit in consecutive breaths.

Second, ayah 29 removes the comfort of ignorance. The Reminder had already come — Ibn Kathir's gloss is that it had already reached him. Knowing the truth is not the finish line.

Third, the passage is anchored by a Name — *ar-Raḥmān*, whose sovereignty on that Day is the true one (ayah 26). The Day is described as hard on the disbelievers, and it is the same Day of which Allah says of the believers, *"The greatest terror will not grieve them"* (21:103). The regret described here belongs to a man who has run out of time. Anyone reading these ayat has not.

passages.title: A Quran abandoned, and why it came piece by piece
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** In ayah 30 the Messenger ﷺ turns to his Lord with a complaint that has echoed ever since: *my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned*. Everything that follows answers that complaint. Ayah 31 consoles him — every prophet before him faced the same enemies. Ayat 32–33 answer the specific objection the deniers used to justify turning away: why did this Book not come down in one piece? And ayah 34 shows where the road of that objection ends.

The thread running through all five ayat is the Qur'an itself: a Book abandoned by those who should have embraced it, defended by the One who sent it, and delivered piece by piece precisely so that the heart carrying it would not break.

## Ayah 30: the Messenger's complaint

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah tells us how His Messenger and Prophet Muhammad ﷺ will say, "O my Lord! Verily, my people deserted this Qur'an."

The idolaters would not listen to it. Ibn Kathir points to Allah's own description of their tactic elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"And those who disbelieve say: 'Listen not to this Qur'an, and make noise in the midst of it'"* (41:26). Ibn Kathir explains what that looked like in practice: when the Prophet ﷺ would recite the Qur'an to them, they would talk nonsense or start speaking about something else, so that they would not hear it.

Picture that. Not an argument, not a rebuttal — just noise, deliberately raised so that the words could not land. That is the first and crudest form of abandoning the Qur'an.

**When was this complaint made?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a genuine difference of opinion among the commentators: is this a complaint the Prophet ﷺ will make on the Day of Judgement, or one he made during his lifetime? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says both views appear valid, but leans toward the second — because the verse that follows reads as a consolation, which suggests the complaint was made in his lifetime and the next ayah came down to settle his heart. Ibn Kathir renders it in the future tense: "the Messenger *will say*." Where the scholars have genuinely differed, it is honest to hold both and see the weight of each.

## What "abandoning the Qur'an" actually means

This is the heart of the passage, and Ibn Kathir does something remarkable here. Rather than confining "abandonment" to the loud dismissal of the Makkan idolaters, he opens the word out into a series of quieter desertions. In his words, the noise-making of the idolaters is one form of forsaking the Qur'an and rejecting it — **and then**:

- **not believing in it** is the same as forsaking it;
- **not pondering its meanings and trying to understand it** is the same as forsaking it;
- **not acting upon it**, following its commandments and heeding its prohibitions, is the same as forsaking it;
- **turning away from it in favour of poetry or other words or songs or idle talk or some other way** is the same as forsaking it.

Read that list slowly. Each step is a smaller distance from the Book than the one before, and Ibn Kathir gives each the same name. A person may never mock a single ayah and still, by his measure, be counted among those who have forsaken it.

Ibn Kathir does not end that passage with a rebuke but with a prayer, and it is worth carrying: he asks Allah, the Most Generous, the Bestower of bounty, the One able to do what He wills, to keep us safe from doing what earns His wrath and to use us for what earns His pleasure — the preserving and understanding of His Book, and following its commandments night and day in the manner He loves and which pleases Him, for He is Generous and Kind.

## A warning meant for us, not only for them

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection: on the face of it, "abandoning" the Qur'an means denying it or refusing to accept it, and that is what you would expect from disbelievers, not from Muslims. But it then reports that in certain narrations, Muslims who *do* believe in the Qur'an and yet neither read it nor try to follow it fall as much within the reach of this same description.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Sayyidnā Anas ؓ as reporting that the Prophet ﷺ said that the person who has learnt the Qur'an and then hung it up — neither reciting it routinely nor pondering over its injunctions — will be brought on the Day of Resurrection with the Qur'an hanging from his neck by a sling, complaining before Allah: *"This servant of Yours had abandoned me, so decide between me and him."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the source of this report as Qurṭubī.

Notice the terrible symmetry with ayah 30. In ayah 30 it is the Messenger ﷺ who complains that the Book was abandoned. In this report it is the Book itself that complains — and the complaint is against a believer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's heading is blunt: **abandoning the following of the Qur'an is a great sin.**

## Ayah 31: you are not the first

*"Thus have We made for every Prophet an enemy among the criminals."*

Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: just as there are for you, O Muhammad ﷺ, those people who scorned the Qur'an, so in all the previous nations did Allah make for every Prophet an enemy among the criminals — people who called others to their misguidance and disbelief. He connects this to Allah's words, *"And so We have appointed for every Prophet enemies — Shayāṭīn among mankind and Jinn"* (6:112).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the pastoral point: if your adversaries do not accept the Qur'an, this is nothing new. In the past too, people defied Our message, and the messengers had to contend with that. The best course for you as well, it says, is to be contented.

There is a specific kind of comfort here. The ayah does not promise that the opposition will stop; it reframes it. Opposition is not evidence that something has gone wrong with the mission — it is what every prophet met. And the word Allah uses for the enemies is *al-mujrimīn*, the criminals: it locates the fault in them, not in the message or the one carrying it.

**"But sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and Helper."** Ibn Kathir explains that for the one who follows His Messenger and believes in His Book, Allah will be his Guide and Helper in this world and the Hereafter. And he explains why these two names in particular: the idolaters used to try to prevent people from following the Qur'an lest anyone be guided by it — they wanted their way to prevail over the way of the Qur'an. So Allah answers their scheme point for point. They block guidance; He is the Guide. They fight to make their way win; He is the Helper. And the ayah's own word — *sufficient* — closes the matter: when Allah is your Guide and your Helper, nothing further is needed.

## Ayah 32: "Why was it not sent down all at once?"

Ibn Kathir frames this as one item in a long catalogue: Allah tells us about the many objections raised by the disbelievers, their stubbornness, and how they spoke of things which were none of their concern. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the sequence of objections and answers, which began at the start of the sūrah, is still continuing here.

What exactly were they asking? Ibn Kathir spells it out: why was this Qur'an, which was revealed to him, not sent down all at one time, as the previous Books were — the Tawrāh, the Injīl, the Zabūr and the other Divine Books? It sounds like a scholarly question. It was not. It was a demand that revelation conform to their expectations, and behind it lay the suggestion that a Book arriving in instalments was somehow less than a Book handed down complete.

Allah's answer does not apologise. It reveals the purpose: *"Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby. And We have revealed it to you gradually, in stages."*

Ibn Kathir explains that it was revealed in stages over twenty-three years, according to events and circumstances and whatever rulings were needed, in order to strengthen the hearts of the believers — and he links this to *"And (it is) a Qur'an which We have divided (into parts)"* (17:106).

On the closing words *wa rattalnāhu tartīlā*, Ibn Kathir preserves two readings from the early authorities: **Qatādah** said it means "We have explained it," and **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam** said it means "We have given its interpretation." So the staged delivery is not merely a schedule — on these two readings it is bound up with the Book being made clear.

## How coming in pieces strengthened the heart

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the mechanism in three concrete ways:

**1. It made memorisation possible.** It was made easy for him to remember the Qur'an by heart; if the whole Book had been revealed in one go, holding it by heart would not have been that easy. And remembrance of the Qur'an by heart, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, expelled all worries from his heart.

**2. It matched the medicine to the wound.** Whenever the disbelievers raised an objection or inflicted some mistreatment, a verse would be revealed to give him fortitude. Had the entire Qur'an been revealed in one piece with the fortitude for that special occasion mentioned somewhere inside it, searching it out would have been painstaking — and it would have been uncertain whether or not his attention would be drawn to the particular verse.

**3. The timing itself was the proof.** An instant response by way of revelation, answering awkward questions, was by itself the confirmation of Allah's support — and that, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is the biggest source of strength for the heart.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a careful qualification: the wisdom of keeping the heart strong is not dependent on gradual revelation alone. Other factors are mentioned elsewhere, as in *"And We have divided the Qur'an into portions, so that you may recite it to the people gradually"* (17:106). (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Bayān ul-Qurʼān here.)

**The two descents.** Ibn Kathir records that Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Nasāʼī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The Qur'an was sent down all at once to the first heaven on Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power), then it was revealed over twenty years." So there is a sense in which the Qur'an *did* descend complete and in one act — to the first heaven, on Laylat al-Qadr. What reached the Prophet ﷺ in instalments was its release into the life of a man and a community.

## Ayah 33: the promise that no argument will stand

*"And no example or similitude do they bring, but We reveal to you the truth, and the better explanation thereof."*

Ibn Kathir explains "no example or similitude do they bring" as meaning no arguments or doubts. And the answer: they do not say anything in an attempt to oppose the truth without Allah responding to them with the truth of that same matter — more clearly and more eloquently than anything they say.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees this ayah as supporting and accentuating the wisdom just described: it promises Allah's support in any situation of awkward questions asked by the deniers. Read the two ayat together and the logic locks: *why is it coming piece by piece?* Because each piece is an answer arriving exactly when it is needed — and here is the guarantee that no challenge will ever arrive without its answer.

Look closely at what is promised. Not merely a rebuttal, but *aḥsana tafsīran* — "the better explanation." The reply Allah supplies does not just neutralise the objection; it comes more clearly and more eloquently than anything the objectors said. This is the confidence a believer can carry into any conversation about this Book.

## Ayah 34: where that road ends

*"Those who will be gathered to Hell on their faces, such will be in an evil state, and most astray from the path."*

Ibn Kathir marks the turn: Allah now tells us about the terrible state of the disbelievers when they are raised on the Day of Resurrection and gathered into Hell. His heading over this whole section names the three movements together — the reason the Qur'an was revealed in stages, the refutation of the disbelievers, and their evil end.

Ibn Kathir reports that in the Ṣaḥīḥ, it is reported from Anas that a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, how will the disbeliever be gathered on his face on the Day of Resurrection?" The Prophet ﷺ said: **"The One Who caused him to walk on his two feet is able to make him walk on his face on the Day of Resurrection."**

That answer is worth sitting with. The question assumes a difficulty; the reply removes it by pointing to the One whose power gave the man his walk in the first place. We affirm that power exactly as the ayah and the ḥadīth state it, without likening it to anything in creation and without explaining it away.

## Living it

The passage puts one question in front of a believer, and Ibn Kathir has already framed it: on his reckoning, abandonment is not a single act but a slope, and the last step on it — turning away from the Qur'an in favour of idle talk or amusement — is one almost anyone can take without noticing.

So the practical shape of these ayat is small and daily. **Recite it**, so that it is not a book learnt and then hung up. **Ponder it**, since Ibn Kathir counts failure to seek its meaning as a form of forsaking it in its own right. **Act on it** — its commandments and its prohibitions — because he counts that too. And when the Book asks something hard of you, remember why it came the way it did: piece by piece, timed to the moment, sent by a Lord who is *sufficient* as a Guide and a Helper.
